lines.text: Fragments and Sayings

Everything that survives of Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BCE), founder of the Stoa: his division of philosophy into logic, physics and ethics, the kataleptic impression, fire and the Logos that runs through the cosmos, the end as living in agreement with nature, his Republic, and the sayings remembered of him. Each fragment is given with the ancient author who preserves it. Text of the fragments from A. C. Pearson, The Fragments of Zeno and Cleanthes (Cambridge, 1891), numbered as there; Pearson's commentary is not included. New English translation, with the Greek and Latin beside it; not yet reviewed by a scholar.
Fragments

Fragment 1. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.39 They say that philosophical discourse has three parts: one part of it is physics, another ethics, another logic. Zeno of Citium was the first to divide it in this way, in his work On Reason.
Fragment 2. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.40 Others put logic first, physics second and ethics third; among these is Zeno, in his On Reason.

Fragment 3. Arrian, Discourses of Epictetus 4.8.12 The principles of the philosopher … which Zeno states: to know the elements of reason, what sort of thing each of them is, how they fit together with one another, and whatever follows from them.

Fragment 4. Arrian, Discourses of Epictetus 1.17.10–11 “And logic is unfruitful” … well, we shall look into that. But even if one were to grant this, it is enough that logic is able to discriminate and examine everything else and, as one might say, to measure and weigh it. Who says this? Only Chrysippus, Zeno and Cleanthes?

Fragment 5. Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.2.12 (p. 22, 12 Wachsmuth) Zeno likened the handbooks of the dialecticians to accurate measures that measure out not wheat or anything else of value, but chaff and dung.
Fragment 6. Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 8.2 He (that is, Zeno) used to solve sophisms, and he told his pupils to take up dialectic, since it is able to do this.
Fragment 7. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 7.228, 7.236; cf. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.45 An impression (phantasia) is an imprint in the soul.

Fragment 8. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.50.21; Plutarch, Opinions of the Philosophers 4.8.9 (both to the Stoics generally); Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 8.355; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.70; Cicero, Academica 1.41 Sense-perceptions are true; of impressions, some are true and some false. — Sextus: Democritus overthrew all sensible existence, Epicurus said that everything sensible is reliable, but Zeno the Stoic made a distinction. — Cicero: Arcesilas pressed Zeno hard, since he himself said that everything that appeared to the senses was false, while Zeno said that some impressions were false, but not all. — Cicero: He did not give credence to all impressions.
Fragment 9. Cicero, Academica 1.41 (Zeno) gave credence … only to those impressions which carried a certain distinctive manifestation of the things that appeared.

Fragment 10. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 7.253; 7.227 But the older Stoics say that the criterion of truth is the kataleptic impression. — that the kataleptic impression is the criterion of truth.

Fragment 11. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 7.248 (cf. 7.426; Outlines of Pyrrhonism 2.4); Cicero, Academica 2.18; Augustine, Against the Academics 3.9.18 A kataleptic impression is one that comes from what is, and is stamped and sealed in accordance with that very thing that is, of such a kind as could not come from what is not. — Cicero: …if it were, as Zeno defined it, an impression stamped and moulded from the thing it came from, such as could not come from a thing it did not come from. — Augustine: But let us see what Zeno says: that an impression can be grasped and perceived if it is such that it has no marks in common with a false one.

Fragment 12. Olympiodorus, Commentary on Plato’s Gorgias pp. 53–54 (ed. Jahn) Zeno says that an art is a system made up of apprehensions (katalēpseis) exercised together towards some end useful for the business of life.

Fragment 13. Scholia on Dionysius Thrax, Grammar (Bekker, Anecdota Graeca p. 663, 16) As Zeno too makes clear when he says: “An art is a road-making disposition (hexis), that is, one that produces something by a way and a method.”
Fragment 14. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 7.372–373 (attribution inferred by Pearson) Memory is a storehouse of impressions.

Fragment 15. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 7.151; Cicero, Academica 1.41 Opinion is weak and false assent. — Cicero: from which (ignorance) there arose also opinion, which was weak and shared its nature with what is false and not apprehended.
Fragment 16. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 He used to say that nothing is more foreign to the apprehension of knowledge than conceit.
Fragment 17. Cicero, Academica 1.41 If something had been grasped in such a way that it could not be shaken by argument, he (Zeno) called it knowledge; if otherwise, ignorance.
Fragment 18. Cicero, Academica 1.42 Between knowledge and ignorance he placed apprehension (katalēpsis), and he counted it neither among right things nor among wrong ones.
Fragment 19. Cicero, Academica 1.41 To these impressions, received as it were by the senses, Zeno adds the assent of the mind, which he holds to lie in our power and to be voluntary.
Fragment 20. Cicero, Academica 1.41 And what had been grasped by sense he called by the name “sense” itself.

Fragment 21. Cicero, Academica 1.42 Zeno also put trust in the senses, because an apprehension made by the senses seemed to him both true and reliable: not because it grasped everything that was in the thing, but because it left out nothing that could fall within its scope; and because nature had given it as a kind of standard of knowledge and a starting-point for itself, from which concepts of things were afterwards imprinted on minds; and from these not only first principles but certain broader roads to the discovery of reason are found.
Fragment 22. Cicero, Academica 1.42 Error, rashness, ignorance, opinion and surmise, and in a word everything foreign to firm and steady assent, he excluded from virtue and wisdom.

Fragment 23. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.12.3 (p. 136, 21 Wachsmuth) From Zeno ⟨and his followers⟩. They say that concepts are neither somethings nor qualified things, but figments of the soul that are quasi-somethings and quasi-qualified; and that these were called Ideas by the ancients. For the Ideas are of the things that fall under the concepts, such as men and horses, or, to speak more generally, of all animals and of all the other things of which they say there are Ideas.

Fragment 24. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.13.1c (p. 138, 14 Wachsmuth; Arius Didymus fr. 18 Diels, Doxographi p. 457) Zeno says that a cause is “that because of which”, while that of which it is the cause is an attribute (symbebēkos); the cause is a body, while that of which it is the cause is a predicate. It is impossible for the cause to be present and that of which it is the cause not to obtain. What is said has this force: a cause is that because of which something comes about, as because of prudence comes being prudent, because of soul comes living, and because of temperance comes being temperate. For it is impossible, when temperance is present in someone, for him not to be temperate, or when soul is present, not to live, or when prudence is present, not to be prudent.

Fragment 25. Anonymous, Art of Rhetoric, in Spengel, Rhetores Graeci 1.434, 23 Zeno puts it this way: the narrative is a setting out of the facts of the case, shaped to suit the character presented on the speaker’s behalf.

Fragment 26. Anonymous, Art of Rhetoric, in Spengel, Rhetores Graeci 1.447, 11; Maximus Planudes, in Walz, Rhetores Graeci 5.396 As Zeno puts it: an example is the recalling of something that has happened, for comparison with the matter now under inquiry. — Planudes: An example, as Zeno says, is the recalling of something that has happened, for comparison with the matter now under inquiry.
Fragment 27. Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 4.2.117 Here the words will have to be vivid and, as Zeno would have it, steeped in sense.

Fragment 28. Anonymous mathematical collections, in Hultsch’s edition of Hero’s Geometrica and Stereometrica p. 275 There is a commentary by Taurus of Sidon on Plato’s Republic, which contains the following: Plato defined geometry as … Aristotle as … and Zeno as a disposition in the reception of impressions that cannot be overturned by argument.

Fragment 29. Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 8.1 Against the man who said Judge no case till you have heard both sides Zeno used to argue, employing some such reasoning as this: “Either the first speaker has proved his case, and then the second speaker need not be heard, for the question is settled; or he has not proved it, for it is as if he had not answered when summoned, or had answered with mere twittering. But either he has proved it or he has not; therefore the second speaker need not be heard.”

Fragment 30. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.18 He used to say that the speech of those who avoid solecisms and polish their style is like Alexandrian silver: pleasing to the eye and neatly rounded, just like the coin, but none the better for that. Speech of the opposite kind he likened to Attic tetradrachms: struck carelessly and ungrammatically, yet often outweighing the elegantly written phrases.

Fragment 31. Zonaras, Lexicon, s.v. σολοικίζειν (col. 1662); Cyril, Lexicon (Cramer, Anecdota Parisiensia 4.190) To commit a solecism is not only to be boorish in speech and language, but also in dress, when someone dresses like a rustic, or eats in a disorderly way, or walks about in an unseemly manner, as Zeno says. — Cyril: Solecism: when someone converses without skill. To commit a solecism is not only to be uncouth in diction and speech but also in what one wears, when someone is dressed like a rustic, or eats in a disorderly way, or walks about in an unseemly manner, as Zeno of Citium says.

Fragment 32. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 2.7; Cicero, On Ends 2.17; Cicero, Orator 32.113; Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 2.20.7 So it was that Zeno of Citium, asked how dialectic differs from rhetoric, closed his hand and opened it again and said, “Like this”: by the closing he marked the compact and concise character of dialectic, and by the opening and spreading of the fingers he hinted at the breadth of rhetoric’s power. — Cicero: This is a saying of Zeno the Stoic, I said: all the power of speech, as Aristotle had held before him, is divided into two parts; he used to say that rhetoric is like the open palm and dialectic like the fist, because rhetoricians speak more expansively and dialecticians more compactly. — Cicero: The famous Zeno, founder of the Stoic school, used to show with his hand the difference between these arts: when he had closed his fingers and made a fist, he said dialectic was like that; when he had opened them and spread out his hand, he said eloquence was like the open palm. — Quintilian: So, since there are two kinds of speech, one continuous, called rhetoric, the other concise, called dialectic, Zeno linked them so closely that he likened the latter to a hand clenched into a fist and the former to an open hand.

Fragment 33. Cicero, Academica 2.145 But you say that no one knows anything except the wise man. Zeno used to demonstrate this with a gesture. He would show his open hand with the fingers stretched out and say, “An impression is like this.” Next he would close his fingers a little: “Assent is like this.” Then, when he had closed his hand completely and made a fist, he said that this was apprehension; and from this likeness he gave the thing a name it had not had before, katalēpsis (“grasping”). Then he would bring his left hand up and squeeze that fist tightly and hard, and say that knowledge was like this, and that no one but the wise man possessed it.

Fragment 34. Cicero, Academica 1.39 (Zeno) held that nothing at all could be brought about by a nature that was without body, and that nothing which acts on something, or is acted on, could be anything other than body.

Fragment 35. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.134; Plutarch, Opinions of the Philosophers 1.3.39; Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.10.14 (p. 126, 17 Wachsmuth); Achilles Tatius, Introduction to Aratus p. 124E; Philo, On Providence 1.22; Theodoret, Cure of Greek Maladies 4.12 They hold that there are two principles of the universe, the active and the passive. The passive is unqualified substance, that is, matter; the active is the reason (logos) in it, that is, God. For God, being eternal, fashions each thing throughout all matter. Zeno of Citium sets out this doctrine in his On Substance. — Plutarch: Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, the principles are God and matter, the one being the cause of acting, the other of being acted upon, and that the elements are four. — Stobaeus: Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, the principles are God and matter, and the elements four. — Achilles: Zeno of Citium says that the principles of the universe are God and matter: God the active, matter what is acted upon; and from them the four elements came into being. — Philo: Zeno, son of Mnaseas, air, God, matter and four elements. — Theodoret: Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, pupil of Crates and founder of the Stoic school, said that God and matter are the principles.

Fragment 36. Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies (Philosophumena) 21.1 (Diels, Doxographi p. 571); Galen, History of Philosophy 16 (Diels, Doxographi p. 608) Chrysippus and Zeno, who themselves also laid it down that God is the principle of all things, being the purest body, and that his providence pervades all things. — Galen: Plato and Zeno the Stoic both discussed the substance of God but did not think alike about it: Plato held God to be incorporeal, Zeno held him to be a body; neither said anything about his shape.

Fragment 37. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.36; Epiphanius, Against Heresies 3.2.9 (Diels, Doxographi p. 592) He thinks that a certain reason, extending through the whole nature of things, is endowed with divine power. — Epiphanius: He said that the divine pervades all things.
Fragment 38. Tertullian, To the Nations 2.4 For look, Zeno too separates the matter of the world from God, and says that God has passed through it as honey passes through the honeycomb.

Fragment 39. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.36; Lactantius, Divine Institutes 1.5; Minucius Felix, Octavius 19.10 Zeno holds that the law of nature is divine, and that it has the power to command what is right and forbid the opposite. — Lactantius: Likewise Zeno (calls God) the divine and natural law. — Minucius Felix: Zeno that the natural and divine law … is the principle of all things.
Fragment 40. Philodemus, On Piety ch. 8 … must … the power, which binds the parts fittingly to one another, and … … and the rising of the sun and its circuit or period.

Fragment 41. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1.36; Tertullian, Against Marcion 1.13; Minucius Felix, Octavius 19.10; Cicero, Academica 2.126 He (Zeno) says that the aether is God. — Tertullian: They declared to be gods … as Zeno did air and aether. — Minucius Felix: sometimes that the aether is the principle of all things. — Cicero: To Zeno and nearly all the other Stoics the aether seems to be the supreme God.

Fragment 42. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.1.29b (p. 35, 9 Wachsmuth); Augustine, Against the Academics 3.17.38 Zeno the Stoic (declared God to be) the fiery mind of the world. — Augustine: For he (Zeno) thought that God himself was fire.

Fragment 43. Themistius, Paraphrase of Aristotle’s On the Soul 72b (Spengel 2, p. 64, 25) Perhaps the view also agrees with that of Zeno’s followers, who hold that God has passed through all substance, and is in some places mind, in others soul, in others nature, and in others cohesion (hexis).

Fragment 44. Lactantius, Divine Institutes 4.9 (“On True Wisdom”); Tertullian, Apology 21; Minucius Felix, Octavius 19.10 Zeno proclaims the Logos as the arranger of the nature of things and the craftsman of the universe, and he calls it fate, the necessity of things, God, and the mind of Jupiter. — Tertullian: Among your own sages too it is agreed that the Logos, that is, word and reason, is regarded as the craftsman of the universe. For Zeno defines it as the maker who formed all things in their order, and says that it is also called fate, God, the mind of Jupiter, and the necessity of all things. — Minucius Felix: Zeno calls reason God. — Lactantius: … he calls it , following, of course, the custom by which they take “Jupiter” to mean God.

Fragment 45. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.5.15 (p. 78, 18 Wachsmuth); Theodoret, Cure of Greek Maladies 6.14 Zeno the Stoic, in his On Nature, a power that moves matter in the same respects and in the same way, which it makes no difference whether one calls providence or nature. — Theodoret: Zeno of Citium called fate a power that moves matter, and he named the same thing both providence and nature.
Fragment 45A. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.149 Chrysippus …, Posidonius … and Zeno say that all things come about by fate; but Boethus …

Fragment 46. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.57; Cicero, Academica 1.39; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 3.27; Tertullian, To the Nations 2.2 Zeno, then, defines nature by saying that it is a craftsmanlike fire, proceeding methodically to generation. For he holds that it is above all the mark of an art to create and beget, and that what the hand achieves in the works of our arts, nature achieves far more skilfully; that is, as I said, it is a craftsmanlike fire, the teacher of all other arts. — Cicero: Zeno held that fire is nature itself. — Cicero: … of nature proceeding with craftsmanship, as Zeno says. — Tertullian: Zeno would have nature be like fire.
Fragment 47. Tatian, Address to the Greeks 3 And according to him (Zeno), God will be shown to be the maker of evils, dwelling in sewers and worms and in those who commit unspeakable acts.

Fragment 48. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.58 But the nature of the world itself, which confines and contains all things in its embrace, is said by the same Zeno to be not only craftsmanlike but actually a craftsman, planning and providing for every benefit and every need.

Fragment 49. Chalcidius, Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus 290 Most, however, distinguish matter from substance, as Zeno and Chrysippus do. They say that matter is what underlies all things that have qualities, while substance is the primary matter of all things, their most ancient foundation, by its own nature without features and without form. So bronze, gold, iron and the like are the matter of the things made from them, but not their substance; whereas that which causes both these and everything else to exist is itself substance.

Fragment 50. Chalcidius, Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus 292 Next, Zeno says that this substance is finite, and that it is the one common substance of all things that exist; that it is also divisible and changeable throughout: its parts change but do not perish in such a way as to be consumed from being into nothing. And just as with the countless different figures moulded even in wax, so he holds that the matter which is the foundation of all things has no form, no shape, and no quality at all of its own, yet is always joined to some quality and inseparably bound up with it. And since it is as much without beginning as without end — for it neither came from what does not exist nor will be consumed into nothing — it has never lacked, from all eternity, the breath (spiritus) and vigour that moves it rationally, sometimes as a whole and sometimes in part; and this is the cause of the frequent and violent transformation of the universe. This moving breath, he holds, is not nature but soul, and indeed rational soul, which, giving life to the sensible world, has adorned it to the beauty with which it now shines. This they call a blessed living being and a god.

Fragment 51. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.11.5a (p. 132, 26 Wachsmuth); Epiphanius, Against Heresies 1.5; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.150; Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 7 From Zeno: Substance is the primary matter of all things that exist. It is all eternal and becomes neither more nor less; but its parts do not always remain the same, but are divided and blended together. Through it runs the Logos of the universe, which some call fate, just as the seed does in the generative fluid. — Epiphanius: So he (Zeno) too, like the other sects, calls matter coeval with God, and says that there is fate and a process of becoming by which all things are governed and acted upon. — Diogenes: They say that the substance of all existing things is primary matter, as Zeno … says. “Substance” and “matter” are used in two senses: of all things together and of particular things. The substance of the whole becomes neither more nor less, but that of particular things becomes both more and less. — Tertullian: And where matter is made equal with God, that is the teaching of Zeno.

Fragment 52. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.17.3 (p. 152, 19 Wachsmuth); Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.135–136; 7.142; Probus, Commentary on Virgil p. 10, 33 Keil Zeno declares this explicitly: the ordering of the universe out of substance in each cycle will have to be of this kind. When the change from fire into water takes place by way of air, part of it settles and earth is formed; of the remainder, part stays as water, and from the part that evaporates air comes into being; and as the air is rarefied, fire is kindled. Mixture and blending come about through the change of the elements into one another, one body passing wholly through the whole of another. — Diogenes: God, mind, fate and Zeus are one, and he is called by many other names besides. In the beginning, being by himself, he turned the whole of substance through air into water; and just as the seed is contained in the generative fluid, so he, being the seminal reason (spermatic logos) of the world, remains behind in the moist element, making matter workable for himself for the generation of what follows. Then he first brings forth the four elements: fire, water, air, earth. Zeno speaks of them in his On the Whole. — Diogenes: The world comes into being when substance is turned from fire through air into moisture; then its thicker part, condensing, becomes earth, while its finer part turns to air, and this, rarefied still further, produces fire; then by mixture of these come plants, animals and the other kinds. Zeno speaks of the generation and destruction of the world in his On the Whole … — Probus: The Stoics Zeno of Citium, Chrysippus of Soli and Cleanthes of Assos teach that from these (the four elements) all things were afterwards formed.

Fragment 53. Galen, Commentary on Hippocrates’ On Humours 1 (16.32 Kühn); Galen, On the Natural Faculties 1.2 And Zeno of Citium held that, just like qualities, substances too are blended through and through. — Galen: But if one must hold that substances, just like qualities, are blended through and through, as Zeno of Citium later declared …

Fragment 54. Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.20.1e (p. 171, 2 Wachsmuth); Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 15.18.3; Arnobius, Against the Nations 2.9 Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus hold that substance changes into fire as into a seed, and that from this again the world-order is produced such as it was before. — Eusebius: The Stoic philosophers hold that the whole of substance changes into fire as into a seed, and that from this the world-order is produced again just as it was before; and this doctrine was accepted by the first and oldest members of the school, Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus. — Arnobius: Does not the man who threatens the world with fire, and says it will burn when the time comes, (believe) Panaetius, Chrysippus and Zeno?

Fragment 55. Tatian, Address to the Greeks 5 Zeno, who declares that after the conflagration the same people will rise again to do the same things (I mean Anytus and Meletus to accuse, Busiris to murder strangers, and Heracles again to perform his labours), must be rejected.

Fragment 56. , On the Eternity of the World, chs. 23–24 (p. 510 Mangey; p. 264 Bernays; Diels, Doxographi p. 486) Theophrastus, however, says that those who ascribe coming-to-be and perishing to the world were misled by four very important things: the unevenness of the earth, the retreat of the sea, the dissolution of each of the parts of the whole, and the perishing of land animals by whole kinds. The first they establish as follows: ‘If the earth had not had a beginning of its coming-to-be, no part of it would still be seen standing up; all the mountains would long ago have been brought low and all the hills made level with the plain. For since so many rains have fallen each year from all eternity, it is likely that of the things raised up to a height some would have been torn away by torrents, while others would have subsided and been loosened, and that everything would by now have been smoothed down throughout. But as it is, the continual unevenness and the towering of very many mountains to an ethereal height are signs that the earth is not eternal; for long ago, as I said, in infinite time, the whole of it would have been made a highway from end to end by the downpours. For it is the nature of water, especially when it dashes down from the greatest heights, to hollow things out, partly from outside by its force, partly by pecking at them with the steady succession of its drops, and to work its way through hard-soiled and stony ground no less than diggers do.’ ‘And indeed the sea,’ they say, ‘has already diminished. Witness the most famous of islands, Rhodes and Delos: for these in ancient times had vanished and sunk beneath the sea, flooded over, but later, as the sea gradually diminished little by little, they emerged, as the histories written about them show. Besides this, great and deep gulfs of great seas have dried up and become mainland, and, sown and planted, have become no poor part of the adjacent country; in them certain signs of the ancient covering by the sea have been left behind, pebbles and shells and all such things as are usually cast up on beaches. If, then, the sea is diminishing, the earth too will diminish, and in long periods of years each of the two elements will be entirely used up; the whole air too will be spent, lessening little by little, and all things will be merged into one substance, that of fire.’ To establish the third head they use an argument of this sort: ‘That thing perishes entirely of which all the parts are perishable; but all the parts of the world are perishable; therefore the world is perishable.’ What we postponed must now be examined. What part of the earth, to begin with that, greater or smaller, will not be dissolved by time? Do not the strongest of stones grow damp and rot through the weakness of their holding-state (hexis) , and, crumbling and flowing away, are they not first resolved into fine dust? What next? If water is not fanned by the winds, does it not die of stillness when left unmoved? At any rate it changes and becomes most foul-smelling, like an animal deprived of soul. And the corruptions of air are plain to everyone: it is its nature to fall sick, to waste away, and in a manner to die. For what could one say a pestilence is, aiming not at fine names but at the truth, except the death of air, pouring out its own affliction to the destruction of everything that has a share in soul? Why speak at length about fire? When it is unfed it is at once extinguished, becoming, as the poets say, lame of itself. That is why, when it is propped up, it stands upright according to the supply of the kindled fuel, but when this is consumed it vanishes. If, then, each of the parts of the world undergoes destruction, clearly the world compacted out of them will not be indestructible.’ The fourth and remaining argument, they say, must be set out precisely as follows: ‘If the world were eternal, the animals too would be eternal, and much more so the human race, inasmuch as it is better than the others. But it has also been shown to be late-born to those who wish to investigate the things of nature. For it is likely, or rather necessary, that the arts coexisted with human beings as being of the same age, not only because methodical order is proper to a rational nature, but also because it is impossible to live without them. Let us look at the dates of each, disregarding the myths told in tragic style about the gods * * * if man is not eternal, neither is any other animal, so that neither are the regions that have received them, earth, water and air. From this it is clear that the world is perishable.’

Fragment 57. Philargyrius, Commentary on Virgil's Georgics 2.336 Zeno that, although some things out of this world perish, the world itself nevertheless endures for ever, because the elements from which material things are generated inhere in it; as he said, it grows, but does not come to destruction, since the elements remain from which it regains its strength.

Fragment 58. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.143; Stobaeus, Eclogues 1.22.3b (p. 199, 10) Diogenes Laertius: That (the world) is one, Zeno says in his work On the Whole. — Stobaeus: Zeno that the world is one.

Fragment 59. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 9.101; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.22 Sextus: Zeno of Citium, taking his starting point from Xenophon, argues as follows: That which emits the seed of something rational is itself rational; but the world emits the seed of something rational; therefore the world is rational. And with this its existence is also established. — Cicero: Nothing that is devoid of soul and reason can generate out of itself a living being possessed of reason. But the world generates living beings possessed of reason. Therefore the world is a living being possessed of reason.

Fragment 60. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.22 And he (Zeno) also argued in this way: “No part of anything that lacks sensation can be sentient. But parts of the world are sentient. Therefore the world does not lack sensation.”

Fragment 61. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 9.104; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.21 Sextus: And again Zeno says: “The rational is better than the non-rational; but nothing is better than the world; therefore the world is rational. And likewise with what is intelligent and what partakes of soul. For the intelligent is better than the non-intelligent, and the ensouled better than the soulless; but nothing is better than the world; therefore the world is intelligent and ensouled.” — Cicero: That which uses reason is better than that which does not use reason. But nothing is better than the world. Therefore the world uses reason.

Fragment 62. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 9.107 In effect Plato set out the same argument as Zeno; for he too says that the universe is the most beautiful work wrought according to nature and, by the likely account, a living being, ensouled, intelligent and rational.

Fragment 63. For passion, too, is a bad and intemperate reason, which has gained vehemence and strength from a base and erroneous judgement.

Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.110; Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4.11 and 4.47 Diogenes: According to Zeno, passion (pathos) itself is the irrational and unnatural movement of the soul, or excessive impulse (hormē). — Cicero: This, then, is Zeno’s definition: a disturbance, which he calls pathos, is a movement of the mind turned away from right reason and contrary to nature. Some put it more briefly: a disturbance is an over-vehement appetite. — Again: the definition of disturbance which I think Zeno rightly used; for he defines a disturbance as a movement of the mind turned away from reason and contrary to nature, or more briefly, as an over-vehement appetite.

Fragment 137. Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.7.1 (p. 39.5 Wachsmuth) As Zeno the Stoic defined it: passion is excessive impulse. He does not say ‘naturally apt to be excessive’, but already in excess; for it is so not potentially but actually. He also defined it in this way: passion is a fluttering (ptoia) of the soul, comparing the ready motion of the passionate element to the flight of winged creatures.

Fragment 138. Cicero, Academica 1.38 Zeno wanted the wise man to be free of all these (disturbances), as of diseases… for he held that the disturbances are voluntary and are taken on through a judgement of opinion, and he considered that the mother of all disturbances is a kind of immoderate intemperance.

Fragment 139. Galen, On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 5.1 (Kühn 5.429); 4.3 (Kühn 5.377); 4.2 (Kühn 5.367) Galen: Zeno held that the passions are not the judgements themselves but the contractions and dissolutions, the elations and sinkings of the soul that supervene upon them. — Again (Chrysippus contradicts Zeno and other Stoics), who suppose that the passions of the soul are not the judgements themselves but the irrational contractions, humiliations and bitings, elations and expansions that follow upon them. — Again: Epicurus… and Zeno suppose the essence of the passions to be of this kind (namely, that the diminutions, elations, contractions and expansions… are affections of the irrational power, supervening upon opinions).

Fragment 140. Themistius, On the Soul 90b (Spengel 2.197.24) And the followers of Zeno do not do badly in holding that the passions of the human soul are distortions of reason and mistaken judgements of reason.

Fragment 141. Galen, On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 3.5 (Kühn 5.322) Not only Chrysippus but also Cleanthes and Zeno readily posit them (namely, that fears and griefs and all such passions arise in the heart).
Fragment 142. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.110 Of the passions, the highest genera (as Zeno says in his work On the Passions…) are four: grief, fear, desire and pleasure.

Fragment 143. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3.74–75; Galen, On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato 4.7 (p. 416) Cicero: I think it has been sufficiently stated that distress is the opinion of a present evil, an opinion which includes the belief that one ought to feel distress. To this definition Zeno rightly adds that this opinion of a present evil must be recent. — Galen: ‘This definition of grief, at any rate,’ he says, ‘like many other definitions of the passions stated by Zeno and written down by Chrysippus, clearly refutes his view. For he says (? they say) that grief is a fresh opinion that evil is present to oneself. And sometimes, putting it more concisely, they express it thus: grief is a fresh opinion of the presence of evil.’

Fragment 144. Lactantius, Divine Institutes 3.23; Lactantius, Epitome (Letter to Pentadius) 38 Lactantius: He (Zeno) places pity among vices and diseases. — Again: Zeno, master of the Stoics, who praises virtue, judged pity… to be a disease of the mind.

Fragment 145. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.107–108 and 7.25; Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.7.8 (p. 85.13 Wachsmuth); Cicero, On Ends 3.58 Diogenes: Further, they say that an appropriate act (kathēkon) is that which, when done, admits of a reasonable justification — for example, what is consistent in life; and this extends even to plants and animals, for appropriate acts are seen in them too. The appropriate act was first so named by Zeno, the term being taken from ‘coming upon (befitting) certain persons’ (kata tinas hēkein). — Again: They say he was the first to use the name ‘appropriate act’ and to write a treatise about it. — Stobaeus: The appropriate act is defined as what is consistent in life, which when done has a reasonable justification; and the inappropriate as the opposite. This extends even to irrational animals, for they too act in some way consistently with their own nature; but in the case of rational animals it is rendered thus: what is consistent in one’s way of life. — Cicero: An appropriate act (officium) is one so done that a probable reason can be given for doing it.
Fragment 146. Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.7.1 (p. 38.15 Wachsmuth) The followers of Zeno the Stoic define it figuratively: character (ēthos) is the spring of life, from which individual actions flow.
Fragment 147. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.173 According to Zeno, character can be grasped (is kataleptic) from outward appearance.

Fragment 148. Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.7.11g (p. 99.3 Wachsmuth) For Zeno and the Stoic philosophers who followed him hold that there are two classes of men, the good (spoudaioi) and the bad (phauloi); and that the good use the virtues throughout their whole life, the bad the vices. Hence the one class always acts rightly in everything it undertakes, the other errs. And the good man, using his experience of life in what he does, does everything well — that is, prudently, temperately and in accordance with the other virtues — while the bad man, on the contrary, does everything badly. And the good man is great, robust, lofty and strong: great, because he is able to attain the things that lie within his purpose and that he has set before himself; robust, because he has grown to full stature on every side; lofty, because he has attained the height that befits a noble and wise man; and strong, because he has acquired the strength that befits him, being invincible and unconquerable. Therefore he is neither compelled by anyone nor compels anyone, neither hindered nor hindering, neither forced by anyone nor himself forcing anyone; he neither masters nor is mastered, neither harms anyone nor is himself harmed, neither falls into misfortunes <nor makes another fall into them>, is neither deceived nor deceives another, is never mistaken nor ignorant nor unaware of himself, nor in general holds any false belief. He is supremely happy, fortunate, blessed, prosperous, pious, dear to the gods and worthy of honour, fit to be king, general, statesman, manager of a household and maker of money. The bad have all the qualities opposite to these.

Fragment 149. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.33; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 5.14.95 Diogenes: Again, in the Republic (Zeno) represents only the good as citizens, friends, kinsmen and free men. — Clement: And Zeno the Stoic, taking it from Plato, as Plato took it from the barbarian philosophy, says that all the good are friends of one another.
Fragment 150. Cicero, For Murena 61 that only the wise are beautiful, even if they are utterly misshapen.

Fragment 151. Cicero, On Ends 5.84; Cicero, For Murena 61 Cicero (On Ends): Zeno dared to call the wise man not only happy but also rich. — Cicero (For Murena): that only the wise are rich, even if they are utter beggars.

Fragment 152. Cicero, For Murena 61 that the wise man is never moved by favour and never pardons anyone’s offence; that no one is merciful except a fool and a trifler; and that it is not a man’s part to be entreated or appeased.

Fragment 153. Cicero, For Murena 61; Lactantius, Divine Institutes 3.4; Cicero, Academica 2.113; Augustine, Against the Academics 2.11 Cicero (For Murena): that the wise man never opines, never regrets anything, is never deceived in anything, and never changes his mind. — Lactantius: If, then, nothing can be known, as Socrates taught, and one ought not to opine, as Zeno taught, the whole of philosophy is done away with. — Cicero (Academica): that the wise man opines nothing… neither of these was strongly maintained before Zeno. — Augustine: …since they had learned from the same Zeno that nothing is more shameful than to opine.

Fragment 154. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.32 (They say that) he (Zeno) calls all who are not good foes, enemies, slaves and strangers to one another — parents to children, brothers to brothers, kinsmen to kinsmen.
Fragment 155. Cicero, For Murena 61 that we, on the other hand, who are not wise, are runaway slaves, exiles, enemies — in short, madmen.

Fragment 156. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 4.158B It is a Stoic doctrine that the wise man will do everything well, and will even season lentil soup wisely. That is why Timon of Phlius said: and one who has not learned to boil a lentil soup wisely — as though lentil soup could not be boiled except according to the instructions of Zeno, who said: Into the lentil soup throw a twelfth part of coriander.

Fragment 157. Philo, That Every Good Man Is Free, p. 880 It is fitting to add Zeno’s saying, that you could sooner sink a wineskin full of air than force any good man, against his will, to do anything he does not wish; for the soul which right reason has braced with firm doctrines is unyielding and invincible.

Fragment 158. Seneca, On Anger 1.16.7 For, as Zeno said, even in the mind of the wise man a scar remains when the wound has healed. So he will feel certain hints and shadows of the passions, but he will be free of the passions themselves.
Fragment 159. Seneca, Letters 83.8 No one entrusts a secret to a drunken man; but one does entrust it to a good man; therefore the good man will not be drunk.

Fragment 160. Plutarch, How One May Become Aware of One’s Progress in Virtue 12 Consider, too, what Zeno’s saying amounts to. He held that each person can perceive from his dreams whether he is making progress: if in sleep he sees himself neither taking pleasure in anything shameful nor approving or doing anything terrible or unjust, but the imaginative and emotional part of the soul, dispersed by reason, shines clear as in the transparent depth of a calm sea untroubled by waves.

Fragment 161. Seneca, Letters 104.21 And if you like to live with Greeks as well, spend your time with Socrates and with Zeno: the one will teach you to die if it becomes necessary, the other to die before it becomes necessary.

Fragment 162. Plutarch, On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander 1.6; Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 2.1; John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew 1.4 Plutarch (Alexander): Indeed, the much-admired Republic of Zeno, the founder of the Stoic school, is directed to this one main point: that we should not live in cities or demes, each separated by its own rules of justice, but should regard all men as fellow-demesmen and fellow-citizens, and that there should be one life and one order (kosmos), like a herd grazing together and nourished in a common pasture. Zeno wrote this, shaping as it were a dream or image of a philosopher’s well-ordered society and constitution. — Plutarch (Self-Contradictions): Since, then, much has been written, in theory, by Zeno himself… about government, about ruling and being ruled, about judging and pleading. — Chrysostom: For not as Plato, who composed that ridiculous Republic, and Zeno, and anyone else who wrote a republic or framed laws…

Fragment 163. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.561C; Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 31 Athenaeus: Pontianus said that Zeno of Citium held Eros to be the god who brings about friendship and freedom, and concord as well, and nothing else. That is why he said in his Republic that ‘Eros is a god who works together for the safety of the city.’ — Plutarch: (Lycurgus’ aim was not to leave Sparta ruling a large empire,) but, believing that the happiness of a whole city, as of a single man’s life, comes from virtue and from its concord with itself, he ordered and fitted everything to this end, that the citizens might become free-spirited, self-sufficient and temperate, and remain so for as long as possible. This is the principle that Plato adopted for his Republic, as did Diogenes and Zeno, etc.

Fragment 164. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 5.11.76; Plutarch, On Stoic Self-Contradictions 6.1; Theodoret, Cure of Greek Maladies 3; Epiphanius, Against Heresies 3.36 Clement: Zeno too, the founder of the Stoic school, says in the book of his Republic that one should make neither temples nor statues, since no construction is worthy of the gods; and he does not shrink from writing these very words: ‘There will be no need to build temples; for nothing should be regarded as sacred that is not of great worth and holy; and no work of builders and craftsmen is of great worth or holy.’ — Plutarch: It is also a doctrine of Zeno’s not to build temples to the gods; for a temple not of great worth is not holy, and no work of builders and craftsmen is of great worth. — Theodoret: Seeing this, Zeno of Citium too, in the book of his Republic, forbids building temples and fashioning statues, for he says none of these is a construction worthy of the gods. — Epiphanius: Zeno of Citium, the Stoic, said that one should not build temples to the gods.
Fragment 165. Stobaeus, Florilegium 43.88 Zeno said that cities should be adorned not with votive offerings but with the virtues of their inhabitants.
Fragment 166. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.33 and (they say that he wrote), at about line 200, that neither temples nor law-courts nor gymnasia should be built in cities.

Fragment 167. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.32 Some, however,… finding fault with Zeno on many points, say that at the beginning of his Republic he declares the ordinary course of education (enkyklios paideia) useless.
Fragment 168. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.33 And about money (Zeno) writes thus: that he does not think coinage should be provided either for the purpose of exchange or for travel abroad.

Fragment 169. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 6.233B–C Zeno of the Stoa, holding that everything about them (gold and silver) was indifferent except using them lawfully and well, forbade both choosing and shunning them, but enjoined that one should, in the ordinary course (proēgoumenōs), use what is simple and unsuperfluous; so that people, keeping their soul in a disposition free from fear and from wonder towards everything else that is neither noble nor shameful, may for the most part use the things that are according to nature, and, fearing none of their opposites at all, may abstain from them by reason and not through fear.

Fragment 170. Seneca, On Leisure 3.2; Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind 1.7 Zeno says: the wise man will take part in public affairs unless something prevents him. — Ready and composed, I follow Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus — none of whom, however, entered public life, and none of whom failed to send others into it.
Fragment 171. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.121 And (the wise man) will marry, as Zeno says in his Republic, and beget children.
Fragment 172. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.129 And the wise man will love those young people who show by their outward appearance a natural aptitude for virtue, as Zeno says in his Republic.

Fragment 173. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.563E And in this you imitate the founder of your wisdom, Zeno the Phoenician, who never had to do with a woman but always with boys, as Antigonus of Carystus records in his Life of him. For you are forever repeating that ‘one should love not bodies but the soul.’

Fragment 174. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus 3.11.74 Zeno of Citium seems to sketch the portrait of a young man, and sculpts him thus: ‘Let his face be clean, his brow not drooping, his eye neither wide open nor languishing; let his neck not be thrown back, nor the limbs of his body slack, but held up like those of a man braced with tension (tonos); let him have a mind upright towards reason, quickness and retention of what is rightly said, and postures and movements that give no hope to the licentious. Let modesty and manliness bloom upon him; and let him keep away from the idle loitering at perfumers’, goldsmiths’ and wool-sellers’ shops and other workshops, where men sit the whole day decked out like courtesans, as if sitting in a brothel.’
Fragment 175. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.22 He said that young men should observe complete decorum in their gait, their bearing and their dress.

Fragment 176. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.131 and 7.33 Diogenes: They also hold that among the wise wives should be in common, so that any man may have intercourse with any woman, as Zeno says in his Republic. — Again: and (they say) that in his Republic he lays down, like Plato, that wives are to be held in common.
Fragment 177. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.33 And (Zeno) bids men and women wear the same clothing and keep no part of the body concealed.

Fragment 178. Origen, Against Celsus 7.63 Those who follow the philosophy of Zeno of Citium avoid adultery… on account of the social bond, and because it is contrary to nature for a rational animal to seduce a woman whom the laws have already given to another, and to ruin another man’s household.

Fragment 179. Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism 3.245; Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 11.190 Outlines: Thus Zeno, the founder of their school, in his Discourses (Diatribai), speaking of the upbringing of boys, says among other similar things the following: ‘Have intercrural intercourse no more and no less with a favourite than with one who is not a favourite, nor with females than with males; for different things do not befit or suit favourites and non-favourites, or females and males, but the same things befit and suit them all.’ — Against the Mathematicians: And indeed, on the upbringing of boys, Zeno the founder of the school sets out in his Discourses things of this kind.

Fragment 180. Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism 3.246; Against the Mathematicians 11.191; Outlines of Pyrrhonism 3.205; Plutarch, Table Talk 3.6.1 Outlines 3.246: Concerning piety towards parents, the same man (Zeno), with reference to the story of Jocasta and Oedipus, says that it was not dreadful for him to rub his mother: if, when she was ill, he had helped her by rubbing some other part of her body with his hands, it would be nothing shameful; and if by rubbing other parts he gave her pleasure, putting an end to her distress, and begot noble children by his mother, was that shameful? — Against the Mathematicians: And Zeno, regarding the stories told about Jocasta and Oedipus, says that it was not dreadful to rub his mother. ‘If, when she was ill in body, he helped her by rubbing her with his hands, there was nothing shameful; and if he rubbed her with another part, and so ended her distress, and begot noble children by his mother, what was shameful in that?’ — Outlines 3.205: Zeno of Citium too says that it is not out of place to rub one’s mother’s private part with one’s own, just as no one would say it was wrong to rub any other part of her body with one’s hand. — Plutarch: ‘For my part, by the dog,’ he said, ‘I could have wished that Zeno’s passages on intercrural intercourse had been set down in some symposium or playful piece, rather than in so serious a work as his Republic.’

Fragment 181. Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians 11.190 And again (Zeno): ‘Have you had intercrural intercourse with your beloved?’ ‘Not I.’ ‘Was it that you did not desire to?’ ‘No, I desired it very much.’ ‘But did you desire him to offer himself to you, or were you afraid to ask him?’ ‘No, by Zeus.’ ‘But you asked him?’ ‘Certainly.’ ‘And then he did not oblige you?’ ‘No, he did not.’

Fragment 182. Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism 3.200 And what wonder is it, when even the Cynic philosophers and Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Chrysippus and their followers say that this (intercourse between males) is indifferent?
Fragment 183. Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism 3.206 And indecent conduct, which with us is held accursed, Zeno does not condemn.

Fragment 184. Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus 3.5 What did you think of the writings of Zeno, or of Diogenes and Cleanthes — all that their books contain, teaching cannibalism: that fathers are to be cooked and eaten by their own children, and that if anyone should refuse, or throw away any part of the loathsome food, he who has not eaten is himself to be devoured?
Fragment 185. Epiphanius, Against Heresies 3.36 (He said) that the dead should be thrown to animals or to fire; and that one may have intercourse with boys without restriction.
Fragment 186. Cicero, Letters to Friends 9.22.1 Yet this (freedom of speech) was Zeno’s view… but, as I say, the Stoics hold that each thing should be called by its own name.

Fragment 187. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 2.20.125 Zeno spoke well about the Indians when he said that he would rather see a single Indian being roasted alive than learn all the proofs about pain.

Fragment 188. Galen, On the Diagnosis and Cure of the Soul’s Passions (Kühn 5.13) So Zeno too thought that we should do everything carefully, as people who will shortly have to give an account of themselves to their tutors (paidagōgoi); for that is what he called most men, who are ready to censure their neighbours even when no one invites them to.
Fragment 189. Stobaeus, Florilegium 14.4 (= Antonius Melissa 1.52) Examine yourself, whoever you are; do not listen to what is said to please you, and strip flatterers of their freedom of speech.

Fragment 190. Maximus the Confessor, Florilegium ch. 6 (ed. Mai) The farmer makes himself useful to those plants from which he wishes to get abundant and fine fruit, and cares for and tends them in every way; and much more are men disposed by nature to show favour to those who are useful to them, and to take the greatest pains over such people; and there is nothing surprising in this. For of the parts of our body too we take more care of those we consider more useful to us for service. So likewise we must be useful, in deeds and not in words, to those from whom we expect to receive benefits. For the olive tree does not preen itself before the man who tends it, but by bearing abundant and fine fruit it persuades him to take more care of it.

Fragment 191. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.565D That wise Zeno, as Antigonus of Carystus says, foretelling, as was natural, your way of life and your affected manners, said that those who misheard his words and failed to understand them would become dirty and mean-spirited, just as those who went astray from the school of Aristippus became profligate and brazen.

Fragment 192. Stobaeus, Florilegium 6.62 For Zeno’s saying, he said, is well put: that one should cut one’s hair for the same reason as one lets it grow, namely for the sake of what is according to nature, so that one may not be weighed down or hampered by one’s hair in any activity.

Fragment 193. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 8.48 Moreover, he (Pythagoras) was the first to call the heaven a kosmos and the earth round — though according to Theophrastus it was Parmenides, and according to Zeno, Hesiod.
Fragment 194. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.91 Zeno of Citium, in his Anecdotes (Chreiai), says that he (Crates) once sewed a sheepskin onto his threadbare cloak (tribōn), heedless of how it looked.

Fragment 195. Dio Chrysostom, Discourses 53.4 Zeno the philosopher too has written on the Iliad and the Odyssey, and on the Margites as well; for this poem too seems to have been composed by Homer when he was younger and was testing his natural gift for poetry. Zeno finds fault with nothing in Homer, explaining and showing at the same time that he wrote some things according to opinion and others according to truth, so that he may not appear to contradict himself in certain passages that seem to be stated inconsistently. This principle — that some things are said by the poet according to opinion and others according to truth — belongs earlier to Antisthenes; but he did not work it out, whereas Zeno set it out in each particular case.

Fragment 196. Plutarch, Commentary on Hesiod 9; Themistius, Orations 8.108c and 13.171d Plutarch: Zeno the Stoic transposed the lines, saying: That man is best of all who heeds one who speaks well; and good, in turn, is he who himself perceives all things — giving first place to ready obedience (to good advice), and second to wisdom. — Themistius: I too am very well pleased with Zeno of Citium, who declared ready obedience to be a more kingly virtue than sagacity, and reversed Hesiod’s order, etc. — Again: For Zeno of Citium rightly held ready obedience to be more kingly than sagacity.

Fragment 197. Plutarch, How the Young Man Should Listen to Poetry 33E And Zeno, correcting the lines of Sophocles, Whoever goes to traffic with a tyrant is his slave, even if he comes there free, rewrote them: is not his slave, if he comes there free, meaning by ‘free’ here the man who is fearless, high-minded and unhumbled.
Fragment 198. Strabo, Geography 7.3.6 (Homer never mentions Arabia) unless we are to heed Zeno the philosopher, who writes the line: I came to the Ethiopians and the Sidonians and the Arabians.

Fragment 199. Stobaeus, Florilegium 95.21 Zeno said that Crates, sitting in a shoemaker’s shop, was reading aloud the Protrepticus that Aristotle wrote to Themison, king of the Cypriots, saying that no one had greater advantages for the pursuit of philosophy, for he had very great wealth to spend on it, and reputation besides. And while he was reading, Zeno said, the shoemaker listened attentively as he went on with his stitching; and Crates said: ‘I think, Philiscus, that I shall write a Protrepticus to you; for I see that you have more advantages for the pursuit of philosophy than those Aristotle wrote of.’
Fragment 200. Stobaeus, Florilegium 36.26 Zeno used to say that of his pupils some were lovers of reason (philologoi), others lovers of talk (logophiloi).
Fragment 201. Stobaeus, Florilegium 6.34 Zeno used to reproach most people, saying that, when they could get their pleasures from toil, they take them from the cookshops.

Fragment 202. Stobaeus, Florilegium 4.107 Zeno said it was absurd that each person pays no heed to the instructions (?) on how one ought to live, on the ground that those who give them do not know, yet admires praise from all and sundry as though it rested on judgement.
Sayings (Apophthegmata)

Saying 1. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.2 (the same in the Suda, s.v. συγχρωτίζεσθαι) When he (Zeno) consulted the oracle about what he should do to live the best life, the god answered: if he took on the complexion of the dead. Understanding what this meant, he read the works of the ancients.

Saying 2. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.3; Themistius, Orations 23.295d Diogenes Laertius: He had been shipping purple dye from Phoenicia and was shipwrecked near the Piraeus. Going up to Athens, by then thirty years old, he sat down beside a bookseller; and as the bookseller was reading aloud the second book of Xenophon’s Memorabilia, he was delighted and asked where men of that sort were to be found. Just then, as it happened, Crates was passing by, and the bookseller pointed to him and said, “Follow this man.” — Themistius: The story about Zeno is well known and told by many: that the Apology of Socrates brought him from Phoenicia to the Painted Stoa.

Saying 3. Plutarch, How to Profit by One’s Enemies 2; Plutarch, On Tranquillity of Mind 6; Suda s.v. νῦν εὐπλόηκα; Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind 14.2 Plutarch (On Enemies): Zeno, when his merchant ship was wrecked and he heard the news, said: “Well done, Fortune, driving us into the philosopher’s cloak!” — Plutarch (On Tranquillity): Zeno of Citium had one cargo ship left; and when he learned that it had gone down, cargo and all, swamped by the sea, he said: “Well done, Fortune, driving us into the philosopher’s cloak and the Stoa!” . — Suda: “Now I have had a good voyage, since I have been shipwrecked”: said of those who have prospered beyond expectation. For Zeno of Citium said this, after leaving his former teachers and becoming a pupil of Crates the philosopher: having met with shipwreck, and saying, “Fortune does well, driving us towards philosophy” * * * thus to have turned to philosophy. — Seneca: When news of the shipwreck came, our Zeno, hearing that everything he owned had sunk, said: “Fortune bids me to philosophize with less baggage.”

Saying 4. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.19 To a man who said that Antisthenes mostly did not please him, he cited a maxim (chreia) of Sophocles and asked whether he thought Antisthenes had anything good in him too. When the man said he did not know, Zeno said: “Then are you not ashamed to pick out and remember whatever bad thing Antisthenes said, but not even to try to retain whatever good thing he said?”

Saying 5. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.20 When someone told him that Polemon set out one subject and then talked about another, he scowled and said: “Well, how much were you paying for what was being given you?”

Saying 6. Plutarch, How One May Become Aware of One’s Progress in Virtue 6; Plutarch, On Praising Oneself Inoffensively 17 Plutarch (On Progress): Zeno, seeing Theophrastus admired for having many pupils, said: “His chorus is larger, but mine is more harmonious.” — Plutarch (On Self-Praise): Thus Zeno, with regard to the great number of Theophrastus’ pupils, said: “His chorus is larger, mine more harmonious.”

Saying 7. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.24 Apollonius of Tyre says that when Crates was dragging him by his cloak away from Stilpo, Zeno said: “Crates, the right way to take hold of philosophers is by the ears. So persuade me and drag me off that way. If you use force on me, my body will be with you, but my soul with Stilpo.”
Saying 8. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.21 He also used to say that most philosophers are unwise in most things, and ignorant of small and chance matters.

Saying 9. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.20 When someone said that the philosophers’ little arguments seemed to him too short, he said: “You are right. Indeed, even their syllables ought to be short, if possible.”

Saying 10. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.25 And when a dialectician showed him seven dialectical forms in the argument called the Reaper, he asked how much he charged for them; and on hearing “a hundred drachmas,” he gave him two hundred.

Saying 11. Suda s.v. δέλτος = Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.37; Plutarch, On Listening to Lectures 18 Diogenes Laertius: Cleanthes, whom Zeno likened to tablets of hard wax, which are written on with difficulty but keep what is written on them. — Plutarch: Just as Cleanthes and Xenocrates, who seemed slower than their fellow students, did not run away from learning or grow weary of it, but were the first to make fun of themselves, comparing themselves to narrow-mouthed jars and bronze tablets, since they took in the teachings with difficulty but kept them safely and firmly.

Saying 12. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.18 When his pupil Ariston was holding forth at length without talent, and in some things rashly and boldly, he said: “Impossible, unless your father begot you when he was drunk.” For this reason he called him a chatterbox, being himself a man of few words.

Saying 13. Stobaeus, Florilegium 36.23; Plutarch, Life of Phocion 5.2 Stobaeus: One of the young men in the Academy was talking foolishly about ways of life. Zeno said: “Unless you dip your tongue in mind before you speak, you will make many more mistakes still in your words.” — Plutarch: Zeno used to say that the philosopher should dip his words in mind before uttering them.

Saying 14. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.20 He said that one who argues should, like actors, have a loud voice and great power, but should not open his mouth wide; that is what people do who talk a great deal, but to no effect.

Saying 15. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.20 He said that things well said should not be left room to be admired, as the works of good craftsmen are; on the contrary, the listener should be so absorbed in what is being said that he has no time to remark on it.

Saying 16. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.22 He said one should not memorize the sounds and words, but occupy the mind with the arrangement of the maxim, not taking it in as one learns some recipe for boiling or preparing food.
Saying 17. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 He said that beauty is the flower of temperance.
Saying 18. Stobaeus, Florilegium Monacense 196 Zeno the philosopher, when some people said that what he said was contrary to opinion, replied: “But not contrary to law.”

Saying 19. Plutarch, On Moral Virtue 4 And yet they say that Zeno too, going up to the theatre when Amoebeus was singing to the lyre, said to his pupils: “Let us go, so that we may learn what harmony and what sound guts and sinews, wood and bones give forth when they partake of reason, number and order.”

Saying 20. Stobaeus, Florilegium 36.19; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 Stobaeus: Zeno, to one who wanted to talk more than to listen: “Young man,” he said, “nature has given us one tongue but two ears, so that we may hear twice as much as we speak.” — Diogenes Laertius: To a youth who was babbling, he said: “This is why we have two ears and one mouth: so that we may hear more and speak less.”
Saying 21. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.21 When a young man was talking a great deal, he said: “Your ears have run down into your tongue.”
Saying 22. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.26 He used to say that it is better to slip with the feet than with the tongue.

Saying 23. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.14 When a crowd stood around him, he pointed in the Stoa to the wooden rail at the top of the altar and said: “This once stood in the middle, but because it was in the way it was set apart by itself. So you too, if you take yourselves out of the middle, will bother us less.”
Saying 24. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.24 Asked how he felt about abuse, he said: “As if an ambassador were sent away without an answer.”

Saying 25. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.24; Stobaeus, Florilegium 33.10; Plutarch, On Talkativeness 4 Diogenes Laertius: Reclining in silence at a banquet, he was asked the reason. He told the man who reproached him to report to the king that there was someone present who knew how to keep silent. Those who asked were ambassadors who had come from Ptolemy and wanted to learn what message they should take from him to the king. — Stobaeus: Zeno, when Antigonus had sent ambassadors to Athens, was invited by them to dinner along with other philosophers; and while the others over the wine were eager to show off their attainments, he himself kept silent. When the ambassadors asked what they should report about him to Antigonus, he said: “Just this, which you see.” For speech is of all things the hardest to control. — Plutarch: At Athens a man entertaining the king’s ambassadors made it his ambition, since they were keen on it, to bring the philosophers together. While the others joined in the talk and contributed their share to it, Zeno kept quiet; so the strangers, greeting him kindly and drinking his health, said: “And what should we tell the king about you, Zeno?” He replied: “Nothing else than that there is an old man in Athens who can keep silent over his wine.”

Saying 26. Aelian, Varia Historia 9.26 King Antigonus held Zeno of Citium in very great respect and esteem. Once, when he was overfull of wine, he burst in on Zeno like a reveller, kissing and embracing him, as drunk men do, and begged Zeno to give him some command, swearing with youthful bravado that he would not fail to grant the request. Zeno said to him: “Go and vomit.” With dignity and greatness of mind at once he rebuked his drunkenness, and spared him from bursting with excess.

Saying 27. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 2.55f; Galen, That the Faculties of the Soul Follow the Mixtures of the Body 3 (Kühn 4.777); Eustathius, Commentary on Homer’s Odyssey 21.293 (p. 1910.42) Athenaeus: That is why Zeno of Citium too, who was harsh and very quick-tempered with his acquaintances, became pleasant and gentle when he had drunk rather freely of wine. To those who asked about this difference in his manner, he said that he was affected in the same way as lupins: for they too are very bitter before they are soaked, but when steeped become sweet and most agreeable. — Galen: And Zeno, they say, used to say that just as bitter lupins become sweet when soaked in water, so he too was affected by wine. — Eustathius: Zeno of Citium, they say, though otherwise harsh towards his companions, nevertheless became pleasant and gentle if he drank rather more wine, saying that he was affected in much the same way as lupins, which are rather bitter before being soaked, but when steeped become sweet and more agreeable.

Saying 28. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 8.345c (the same in Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.19) Zeno of Citium, the founder of the Stoa, dealt thus with the glutton with whom he lived for a long time, as Antigonus of Carystus says in his Life of Zeno. When a large fish happened to be served and nothing else had been prepared, Zeno took it from the dish and made as if to eat it all himself. When the other stared at him, he said: “What then do you think your companions suffer, if you cannot put up with gluttony for a single day?”

Saying 29. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 5.186d Zeno, when one of the gluttons present stripped off the upper side of a fish as soon as it was served, turned the fish over and stripped it himself, adding (Euripides, Bacchae 1129): “And Ino worked away upon the other side.”

Saying 30. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.17 (see also the Suda s.v. σκιμαλίσω) When two men were reclining below him at a drinking party, and the one next to him was nudging the one below himself with his foot, Zeno nudged him with his knee. When the man turned round, Zeno said: “Well then, what do you suppose the man below you suffers from you?”
Saying 31. Stobaeus, Florilegium 57.12 Zeno the Stoic philosopher, seeing one of his acquaintances distracted by the cares of his farm, said: “Unless you get rid of it, it will be the ruin of you.”
Saying 32. Boissonade, Anecdota Graeca 1, p. 450 (attributed to Zeno in Paris, Cod. Reg. 1168) Live, O man, not only in order to eat and drink, but in order to use life for living well.

Saying 33. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.21 And he used to quote the saying of Caphesias: when one of his pupils was trying to blow loudly, Caphesias struck him and said that the good does not lie in the great, but the great in the good.
Saying 34. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.26 Well-being is attained by small steps, yet it is no small thing.

Saying 35. Plutarch, On Compliancy (De vitioso pudore) 13 There is Zeno’s story: he met a young man of his acquaintance walking quietly along by the wall, and learned that he was avoiding a friend who was asking him to give false testimony for him. “What are you saying, you fool?” he said. “He, unreasonable and unjust, does not fear you or feel ashamed before you; and you do not dare to stand up to him on behalf of what is just?”

Saying 36. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.16–17 As, for instance, what he once said of a dandy: when the man was stepping gingerly over a gutter, Zeno said: “He is right to be wary of the mud, for he cannot see his reflection in it.”

Saying 37. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.19 When a lad was asking a question too subtle for his age, Zeno led him to a mirror and told him to look into it. Then he asked him whether he thought such questions suited a face like that.
Saying 38. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.21 When a young man was arguing rather insolently, he said: “I would not say, my lad, what comes into my mind.”

Saying 39. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.21 To a handsome youth who said that he did not think the wise man would fall in love, he said: “Then nothing will be more wretched than you handsome ones (if we are not going to love you).”
Saying 40. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.22 He used to say that nothing is more unbecoming than conceit, and above all in the young.
Saying 41. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 To a man anointed with perfume he said: “Who is this that smells of a woman?”

Saying 42. Stobaeus, Eclogues 2.31.81 (p. 215.13 Wachsmuth) = Florilegium excerpts from the Florentine MS of John of Damascus 2.13.81 Zeno, asked how a young man might go least astray, said: “If he keeps before his eyes those whom he most honours and stands in awe of.”

Saying 43. Stobaeus, Florilegium 15.12 To those who excused their prodigality by saying that they spent out of great abundance, Zeno said: “Then I suppose you will also pardon cooks if they say they have made the dishes too salty because they had plenty of salt?”

Saying 44. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.17 Being in love with Chremonides, when Chremonides and Cleanthes sat down beside him, he got up. When Cleanthes was surprised, he said: “I hear from good physicians too that the best remedy for inflammation is rest.”
Saying 45. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.18 To a lover of boys he said: “Schoolmasters have no sense, spending all their time among boys; nor have the boys.”

Saying 46. Stobaeus, Florilegium 17.43 Zeno of Citium did not think he should take daintier food even when ill. When the physician treating him told him to eat a young pigeon, he would not put up with it: “Treat me,” he said, “as you would treat Manes.”

Saying 47. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.17 When a Cynic, saying he had no oil in his flask, asked him for some, Zeno said he would not give him any. But as the man went away, he told him to consider which of the two of them was the more shameless.

Saying 48. Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 9.370c (cf. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.32) And it is no wonder that some people swore by the cabbage, since Zeno of Citium too, the founder of the Stoa, imitating Socrates’ oath “by the dog,” used himself to swear “by the caper,” as Empodus says in his Memoirs.

Saying 49. Stobaeus, Florilegium 98.68; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 Stobaeus: Zeno used to say that we are poor in nothing so much as in time. For life is truly short, but art is long, and most of all the art that can heal the diseases of the soul. — Diogenes Laertius: And that we are in want of nothing so much as of time.

Saying 50. Stobaeus, Florilegium Monacense 197; Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 Stobaeus: The same (Zeno), asked what a friend is, said: “Another such as I.” — Diogenes Laertius: Asked who is a friend, he said: “Another I.”
Saying 51. Origen, Against Celsus 8.35 Zeno, to the man who said “May I perish if I do not punish you,” replied: “And may I, if I do not make you my friend.”
Saying 52. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 When Dionysius the Renegade asked him why he was the only one he did not correct, Zeno said: “Because I do not trust you.”

Saying 53. Seneca, On Benefits 4.39.1; Themistius, Orations 21.252b Seneca: “Why then,” says he, “did your Zeno, when he had promised a loan of five hundred denarii to someone and had found him hardly a fit person, persist in lending it, though his friends urged him not to, because he had promised?” — Themistius: When did you let off your debtor, as Zeno of Citium did?
Saying 54. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 They say he was flogging a slave for theft; and when the slave said, “It was fated that I should steal,” Zeno said: “And that you should be beaten.”
Saying 55. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.23 Seeing the slave-boy of one of his acquaintances covered with weals, he said to the master: “I see the traces of your anger.”

Saying 56. Diogenes Laertius, Lives 7.28–29; Stobaeus, Florilegium 7.45; Lucian, Long-Lived Men (Macrobii) 19 Diogenes Laertius: He died in this way. As he was leaving the school he tripped and broke his toe. Striking the ground with his hand, he spoke the line from the Niobe: “I come; why do you call me?” and died on the spot, by stopping his breath. — Stobaeus: Zeno, when he was already an old man and had tripped and fallen, said, “I come; why do you call me?” and going indoors, he took his own life. — Lucian: Zeno… who, they say, as he was entering the assembly, stumbled and cried out, “Why do you shout for me?”; and returning home and abstaining from food, he ended his life.
Saying 57. Theodore Metochites, Miscellanea p. 812 Kiessling And Zeno, philosophizing about the affairs of this world and about life, used to say: “It came, it passed; nothing at all to do with me.”
